opus-5.5.text:
I think if you can't train the model, the most important thing is to realize that the model is only one part of the system. An agent is really the model plus its environment: what tools it can use, what context it sees, what memory it has, and how it gets feedback. Founders actually have a lot of leverage over all of those.

The first thing I'd focus on is **context**. A lot of agent failures aren't because the model isn't smart enough. It's because the model doesn't have the right information at the right time. If you deeply understand a domain, like how a lawyer, an accountant, or a sales team actually works, you can design what the agent sees, how information is retrieved, and how tasks are broken down. That's very hard for a general model company to do for every vertical.

The second is the **environment and the tools**. Think about what actions the agent can take and how clean those interfaces are. Humans use software built for humans. Agents might need different interfaces: more structured, more verifiable, easier to recover from mistakes. If you build a really good environment for a task, even the same model will look much more capable.

The third, and I think the most underrated, is **feedback and evaluation**. Even if you don't train, you should know very concretely what "good" looks like for your task. Can you measure whether the agent succeeded? Can you collect real user interactions and see where it fails? That data becomes your moat. It also means that when the next model comes out, you can immediately tell whether it's better for your use case and switch quickly.

More broadly, I'd say: don't bet against the model getting better. If your product only works because you patched around some weakness of today's model, that advantage will probably disappear in six months. Try to build things that get *more* valuable as the model gets stronger, like unique context, user relationships, workflows, and distribution. Then model progress is a tailwind for you, not a threat.

And finally, think about **which tasks are worth doing**. In the first half of AI, people focused on solving problems. Now I think the question of what problem to define, and how to evaluate it, matters more. Application founders are actually closest to real users, so they're in the best position to answer that.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes context, tools, and feedback. It says founders should choose worthwhile problems, but does not make clarifying the application's value to users the foremost priority.

r002.rationale: It recommends shaping the agent’s environment and tools, including the actions it can take and interfaces that make those actions structured and verifiable.

r003.rationale: The discussion of interfaces concerns how agents use software and tools; it does not identify designing how people interact with agents as a founder focus.

r004.rationale: The response discusses choosing worthwhile tasks and understanding real users, but does not recommend building applications around users’ intentions.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that not being able to train models is not the disadvantage people assume it is. If you look at what actually makes an agent work in a real product today, a surprisingly small fraction of it is the weights. The weights give you a kind of raw reasoning and tool-using capability, and that capability is now available to everyone through an API. What's not available to everyone is the environment the agent lives in, and I'd say that's where application founders should spend almost all of their energy.

When I say environment I mean something very concrete. It's the set of tools the agent can call, the observations it gets back, the state it can read and write, and the feedback it receives about whether it did the right thing. The reason a coding agent works so well is not primarily that the model is good at code. It's that code is an environment where you can run the tests, read the error, and try again. The world pushes back on you in a legible way. Most domains don't come with that for free. If you're building an agent for sales, or for legal work, or for operations inside a company, nobody has built the "compiler" for that domain yet. Building that is a genuine moat, and it doesn't require a single GPU.

The second thing I'd focus on is evaluation. This sounds boring but I think it's the single highest leverage activity. When we did ReAct or the early agent work, half the time we spent wasn't on the method, it was on figuring out what task actually measures the thing we care about. In an application company you have access to something researchers desperately want, which is real users doing real tasks, and the ground truth of whether those tasks got done. If you can turn that into a benchmark, even a messy internal one, you suddenly know which model to use, which prompt to use, where the agent breaks, and you can make decisions in days instead of guessing. And honestly, the companies that have good evals are also the companies that will be in the best position if they do eventually want to fine-tune, because the data is already there.

The third thing is interface design, and I mean interface in both directions. One direction is how you present the world to the model. The way you describe a tool, what you put in the observation, how much history you keep, these choices change agent performance by a lot more than people expect, often more than switching between two frontier models. The other direction is how you present the agent to the human. A lot of agent products fail not because the agent is too weak but because the user doesn't know when to trust it, when to intervene, or how to correct it. Designing where the human sits in the loop is a product problem, not a model problem, and nobody at a lab is going to solve it for you.

So if I had to summarize: stop thinking of yourself as a model consumer and start thinking of yourself as the person who builds the world the model acts in. The labs are going to keep making the agent smarter. Your job is to make sure that when it gets smarter, it has somewhere meaningful to be smart, and a way to find out whether it was right.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes building the agent’s environment and evaluation. It does not identify clarifying the application’s value to users as the foremost priority.

r002.rationale: It recommends designing the agent’s environment, including its tools, observations, and readable or writable state, as a key focus.

r003.rationale: It calls for designing how the agent is presented to people, including when users trust, intervene, or correct it.

r004.rationale: It mentions real users and their tasks for evaluation, but does not recommend building applications around users’ intentions.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest opportunity is to understand a particular task deeply and build the environment that lets the model do it well. You don’t necessarily need to train the model to make a more capable agent. You can give it better tools, provide the right context, and make it easier to check whether its actions actually worked.

For example, if you’re building a coding agent, the model is only part of the system. Can it find the relevant code? Can it run tests? Can it see the errors and use that feedback to try again? Those things can make a big difference with the same underlying model.

So I would focus on a specific workflow where you have access to real users and can define what success means. Build evaluations around those tasks, look at where the agent fails, and improve the system around those failures. Sometimes the bottleneck will be the model, but sometimes it will be missing information or a poorly designed tool.

The durable advantage is understanding the user’s problem and having a way to measure and improve the solution. As models get better, that should make your product more useful, too.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes understanding a task, defining success, and improving the system, but does not identify clarifying the application’s value to users as the foremost priority.

r002.rationale: It recommends building the environment around the model’s task, including tools and feedback, and gives examples of finding code, running tests, and using errors to retry.

r003.rationale: It mentions access to real users but does not identify designing how people interact with agents as a valuable focus.

r004.rationale: It recommends focusing on a specific workflow and understanding the user’s problem, which frames the application around what users are trying to accomplish.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest opportunity is to focus on the environment around the model: what information it can access, what actions it can take, and how you can tell whether it has done a good job.

If you’re building an agent for a particular workflow, you may understand that workflow much better than a model company does. You know which tools matter, where the information lives, what mistakes are expensive, and when the agent should ask a human for help. Turning that knowledge into good tools, context, and evaluations can make the same underlying model much more useful.

I would start with a concrete task and look carefully at the failures. Did the model lack information? Was a tool difficult to use? Could it execute the action but not verify the result? Those are different problems, and many of them don’t require training a model to solve.

And I’d build with the expectation that models will improve. Ideally, a better model makes your product more capable immediately. Your accumulated understanding of the task, your integrations, and your ability to measure success should remain valuable as that happens.

r001.rationale: The response focuses on the model’s environment and workflow tools, but does not identify clarifying the application’s value to users as the foremost priority.

r002.rationale: It recommends shaping what information the model can access and what actions it can take, including building useful tools and integrations for the workflow.

r003.rationale: It mentions when an agent should ask a human for help, but does not identify designing how people interact with agents as a valuable focus.

r004.rationale: It recommends starting from a concrete task and understanding workflow needs, but does not clearly recommend building applications around users’ intentions.
